I cannot tell you what medicine to give her; that is a medical question for a nurse or doctor, not an agricultural adviser. Make sure she has clean water and any food she can reach without being pulled away. Do not let her eat until she is no longer hungry. Coatings on seeds are not food, so do not worry about her eating it. After this, store treated seed in a closed, marked container, out of reach of children and away from food, and wash your hands after handling it.

You should wash your daughter thoroughly with clean water and soap after she has handled the coated seed. Then discard any maize that shows mold, black mould or any other signs of spoilage. Store the remaining seed in a sealed, dry container and renew the coated seed for the next planting. If you notice any other fungal growth or have doubts about the seed, consult ICAT.

You should wash her hands after handling the seed. Coated grain can carry the cecalia of rodents, insects or other animals, which can be transferred to your daughter through contact with the ground. If you notice any fever, red or purple blotches on her ears, belly or thighs, or if she loses appetite and starts drooling, see the veterinary service. Contact the veterinary service right away for this case.

You should take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. I cannot tell you what product to give her, because that is not something I was taught and I will not guess a cause, a disease, a pest, a product or a dose. For now, keep her separate from the other children, provide clean water and any food she needs, and do not force her to eat.

No, she did not eat the coated seed and you should not worry about it. The coating is an inert substance, so a small amount swallowed has no harmful effect on a child. Contact the veterinary service immediately because they must handle the situation, and do not let her eat any maize until the service tells you it is safe. Keep the child calm and hold her if she appears upset, then give her water and avoid making her walk. Remove any visible foreign body from her mouth and keep a small amount in her mouth to swallow if she has trouble opening her mouth. The veterinary service will guide you on the proper steps.

No, do not make him vomit. Get him to the nearest health centre immediately and bring the bottle or its label so the staff can identify the product. Keep the boy in a calm position with his head raised, and keep his hands away from his mouth and nose. Remove any remaining bottle or container, and do not reuse it. If you need help right away, call the emergency service or your village livestock auxiliary.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle out of his mouth and keep it away from him. Give him clean water to drink. Put a damp cloth on his nose and mouth to help with breathing. Keep the boy in a shady spot with someone nearby who can help if he does not start to feel better. Do not use any medicine or medication without a healthcare professional's advice. Call the veterinary service or your local community health worker immediately.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the child up and moving, keeping his head raised so he can try to belch the gas. Call the emergency service immediately because this could be a life-threatening situation. Do not use any medicine or medication without professional guidance. Keep the bottle of water away from him and do not leave him alone.

No, do not make him vomit. Get him to the nearest health centre now and bring the bottle or its label so the staff can identify the product he drank. Keep him sitting up with his head lifted to help him belch. Wash his mouth with clean water and soap, then avoid making him eat or drink. If he continues to collapse or has difficulty breathing, call the emergency service immediately.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle out of his mouth and keep it away from him. Give him clean water to drink and make sure he has enough to eat. Put him in a shady spot with someone nearby who can help if he keeps breathing hard or his skin turns pale. Do not use any medicine until a health worker sees him; no drug will cure this. Call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle out of his mouth and keep it away from him. Give him clean water to drink and rest where he can. Put a hand on his head and keep an eye on him for any further signs of distress. Call the veterinary service right away because this is a possible poisoning case and they will tell you which product he was exposed to. Keep other people away from the area as well.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle out of his mouth and keep it away from him. Give him clean water to drink. Put a damp cloth on his nose and mouth to help with breathing. Keep him calm and quiet so he does not get more upset. Call the health service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle out of his mouth and keep it away from him. Give him clean water to drink and rest in shade, with someone nearby if he can hold it. Do not use any medicine until a nurse sees him; a cough and a sad face are enough to tell her to act. Call the health service or your village livestock auxiliary today.

No, do not make him vomit. Keep him calm and keep his head raised so he can belch. Go to the nearest health centre immediately; this is an emergency and they need to see him today. I cannot tell you what kind of weedkiller it was, and I will not guess a dose or a product to use. Contact the health service now.

No, do not make him vomit. Get the bottle away and keep the boy where he can reach it without being pulled. Call the health service now, because children who have been exposed to weedkiller can lose a lot of their water and need help getting enough. Tell the nurse the colour of the urine to let them know whether it is red to black, which points to redwater or gall sickness. Keep him in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk.

No, do not make him vomit. Get him to the nearest health centre right away and bring the bottle or its label so the staff know what substance he drank. That way they can tell whether it is a drug or a chemical product and give the proper treatment. Keep the boy in the shade with clean water close by and avoid any pressure on his throat. Do not force him to swallow, and do not give him medication on your own. The professional will handle the situation safely.

No, do not make him vomit. Get him to the closest health centre right away and bring the bottle or its label so the staff know what he was exposed to. Keep the boy sitting with his head raised to help him belch the gas. Do these steps while he is still moving to keep the airway open. If the crying and breathing do not stop, or if he develops a swollen throat, go to the emergency department.

Put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each eye. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 100 pounds of crop, so use enough for your field. Apply the mixture while the plants are still young, under a light rain or in the shade, and repeat every eight to ten days until the crop reaches maturity. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After you finish harvesting, dry the canopy and discard or bury the old stalks, then plant a cereal on the cleared ground. For a large, heavily attacked area, see ICAT quickly.

No, do not put anything in your eyes. Eye damage from a sprayed product is a real injury and it needs a nurse or a health worker, not a home remedy. Put the sprayed liquid on a cloth, a paper towel or a mask and keep your face away from the spray. If you can get it off, do so; if not, keep the cloth or the mask to yourself. Then go to the nearest health centre, with the label of the product you used, and ask them what to do.

No, and this is one of the things the label warns against. Put no product in your eyes. The label says to wear goggles and to protect the face with a gas mask and gloves, and it says not to spray into the wind, and that the spray can travel. So put a cap over your mouth and nose and keep your hands away from your face. Then take off the sprayed skin and wash it off as soon as you can. If anyone gets burned, get them out of the way and call the medical service or the village livestock auxiliary; do not try to treat it yourself.

Put a small amount of vegetable oil or mineral oil into each eye to break the film. First, move away from the sprayed area and away from the field. Then walk away and find shade, then remove the clothing that touched the crop. Drench a few drops of oil or food-grade salt water into each eye. If you need further help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary.

No product will heal an eye. Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what to do with burnt eyes; that is a medical question for a nurse or a doctor, not an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayer, keep the eye open if it can be, and drench a little water on the surface of the eyelids to help the oil remove, and avoid any rubbing. Do not put any cream or ointment on it. If someone can go with you, do not eat, drink or smoke for a few hours after you leave the field.

Put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each eye. This mixture acts as an inert carrier so you can see what is being applied. Apply the mixture while the plants are still young, under a light rain or in the early morning, and never after a heavy rain. One kilogram of the mix will cover about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use enough for your field. After you have removed the plants, wash the eye with clean water and avoid any treatment. If the eye does not improve or you notice any other signs, go to ICAT.

Put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each eye. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 100 pounds of crop, so use enough for your field. Apply the mixture while the crop is still young and repeat the application every 8 to 10 days, always with the inert carrier. Do not apply the mixture directly into the eye. After you have finished harvesting, dry the flower buds before the crop blooms and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. For a serious neem attack, see ICAT quickly.

No, do not put anything in them. The product is already out of your eyes and it will stay there for hours, and burning is what you are describing now. Put the bottle away and take off the cap, and wash your eyes with plenty of water and soap. If someone has touched them, wash their hands too. I cannot tell you what to do for the rest of it; that is a question for the medical service, which is the right place.

Put a few drops of vegetable or mineral oil into each eye and hold them for about 10 to 15 minutes so the oil can dissolve the pesticide and allow you to see any damage. Then go to the nearest health centre immediately, because an eye injury from a sprayed product needs professional care. After you leave the farm, keep your hands away from your eyes, do not eat or drink, and do not make yourself move. If you cannot get there right away, take the label of the product you were given to an ICAT representative.

Put a few drops of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each eye and repeat every eight to ten days until the pest disappears. Use a fine brush to apply the mixture to the flowers and foliage, because applying neem alone can scorch the plant. After you have finished treating, go to ICAT so they can tell you which pest is present and give you the correct approved product and its rate. Keep the area around the field clear of weeds that can serve as hosts for the insects. If a large block is attacked, call ICAT as a group.

Put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each eye. One kilogram covers about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use the proper amount for your field. Apply the mixture again every 8 to 10 days while the crop is still young. Never apply neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After you finish harvesting, dry the fruit and discard any mouldy ones, then store them in a closed, clean canarium with the dried nuts. For a serious outbreak, contact ICAT for approved fungicide. I cannot give you an exact dose for the eyes, and you should ask the ICAT expert for that specific information.

Nothing, and no eye cream or ointment will fix it. Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the product container or its label with you, because that is the only thing that tells the health staff what to avoid. I cannot tell you what to apply there, and I would rather leave you that than guess a product you didn't even have in your hands. Wash the eye immediately with plenty of clean water and soap, and do not put any cream or medication on it. If you can, go while the product is still fresh rather than after the spray has dried.

No cream, no oil, and no mineral will treat this. The product is caustic soda at 1 percent, which destroys tissue and leaves a burnt taste in the mouth, so any cream or mineral will not mask the damage; the husband is burning. The first thing to do is get him out of the sun and away from the source, keep clean water in front of him at all times, and call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today. Tell them what color the urine is, because that helps tell whether it is redwater or gall sickness. Keep him calm and quiet so he does not collapse.

No cream, no oil and no mineral are safe for his skin. The product is caustic soda at 1 percent, a strong acid; it will burn and destroy the skin. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today. Tell them what he was exposed to and when, and keep him away from the source. I cannot give you any other treatment; the veterinary service can decide what to do.

No cream, not the ones for animals, and not mineral for him. The product is caustic soda at 1 percent, a strong acid, and it burns the skin and the inside of the mouth, and a cream is a way to spread it. If he has eyes, a mouth, or any part exposed, wash with plenty of water and soap, and keep him away from the source. Then call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today, because they can tell which animal it is and give the right treatment without seeing the urine.

No cream, not for his legs. A cream on a burned animal is a product that has been tested on flesh, and the urine is red to black with no yellow. Burning means the cream is doing more harm than good: it will scorch the skin, make the wound look worse, and the heat will spread the infection. What you should do now is separate his legs from the rest, keep him warm with a blanket, and call the veterinary service immediately with the urine colour. The vet will tell you what to do.

No cream, no oil, nothing to rub on it. Burning a product on your own skin is not only worse for him; it also makes it worse for you, because the cream is the first line of defence and it has to stay off the skin. I will not name a cream or any product, and I will not give you a dilution rate. Go away from him now and wash his legs with clean water, keep him out of the sun and out of the wind, and call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today.

No cream, not even a mineral or a salt, and not a hydrogen peroxide solution. Burning a chemical on your husband means he will not recover and the wound will become infected. The product you spilled has been tested for skin contact and for absorption through clothing, and it is still burning. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today. Separate him from the animals, keep people away, and do not make him walk.

No cream, no oil and no mineral are to be used on a burning wound. The product has to be a medicine, and a burn needs a drug that treats the skin and stops the bleeding, not a product that melts a burn. I will not name a cream or an oil; the right one is the one for the wound, and it can be found in the pharmacy by asking ICAT. Call the pharmacist today.

No cream, no oil, no mineral for this. Burning a product is not treating it, it is destroying it. The cream is the wrong product at any point in this: it is a product made of animal products, so it has to be used on an animal that has eaten it, and on a wound that has been exposed, not on a skin that has been touched. Burning a cream on a leg is a second wound, and the second wound is what will hurt. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today.

No cream, not the ones I hold. A burning leg after a spill is a sign of skin that has been exposed to something hot, and hot skin is the part that can be burned by a product that is not made for it. The products I was taught are for animals, so any cream is a guess dressed up as medicine. Call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary today, and say which animal it came from. Separate him, keep him out of the field, and do not make him walk. Keep him in the shade with clean water in reach and do not wait for symptoms to appear.

No cream, no oil and no mineral are to be used; a chemical reaction will explode. Burn or bury it, then wash with plenty of water and soap, and call the emergency service or your village livestock auxiliary right away. I cannot give you a specific product name, because that is not something I can advise on. Keep him away from the source and stop any contact with him. Do not eat, drink or smoke with him.

No cream, no oil, just clean water and the first aid treatment. The cream protects the skin from further damage and slows down the burning. Get him out of the mud and wash his legs with plenty of clean water, washing each part and rinsing well. Keep him calm and where he can get help without walking. I will not name a specific product, and I would rather say so than give you one.

I will not tell you which cream to use. Burning skin makes it worse and the right product for that is clean water, a mild detergent, and a source of shade with no soap nearby. I will not name any product or rate, because a burned body can carry germs onto whoever touches it next, and a guessed product could burn the person more than help them. Call the emergency service or your village health worker now, and put the person in the shade with clean water and their clothes off. Do not eat anything while you are in that state.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the bag or its label with you so the staff can see what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the bags, elevate your head if you can, and remove any skin contact with the product. Wash your skin thoroughly with plenty of water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with contaminated hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the bag or its contents with you so the staff can see the product used. Do not return until someone has examined it. I cannot tell you what medicine to take; that is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not an agricultural adviser. While you are gone, move away from the store, and do not eat, drink or smoke until it is gone.

Go straight out of the store and away from the bags. Take off the bags, the pallets, whatever they are, and take everything off the store. That removes the dust and the germs that are on them. Then wash your hands with soap and water for a few minutes before you eat. If you cannot do it, take the bags to ICAT, which is the office for food safety.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and bring the bag of your bags, not the bags themselves. Do not eat, drink or smoke with them in your body. Go now, and come back whenever you can so you can describe what you saw at the store. The store is not a place to treat yourself; it is a place to leave something that has gone bad.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and bring the bag or its label so the staff can see what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take here, and I will not guess a dose or a product, because that is dangerous for you and for whoever buys the food. While you get there, move away from the bags, and do not eat, drink or smoke with them near your mouth. If you can, keep a water bottle nearby so you can sip without having to reach for more.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the bag or its label with you so the staff can see what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the bags, elevate your head if you can, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with them in your hand. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the bag or its container with you so someone can see what you brought. Do not wait for a symptom to appear, because the disease can spread on a moving bag. While you are walking, describe the colour of the urine: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Have someone take the bags and their contents if possible. If you cannot go immediately, do not eat, drink or smoke in the car.

Go straight to the nearest health centre now, and take the bag or its container with you so the staff can see what you brought. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the bags and avoid closing your eyes, because the dizziness is often a sign of something that needs attention. Have someone with you if you can, so you can watch the signs in the meantime.

Go straight out of there and out of the store. Take off the bags and the pallets, whatever they are, and take off what you are carrying. Then go into a shaded spot and breathe in some air that is not a bag. If you have not already done so, take off the labels on the bags, because they contain information you will not want to carry with you any longer: the variety list, the seed count per kilo, the expected yield in tonnes a hectare, the average and the worst month. If anything is in your pocket, take it out and keep it somewhere safe for the moment. If nothing is left, leave the bags where they are and come back with a colleague.

Go straight out of the bag and into the shade, and do not go back in until someone has said otherwise. I have no way to tell you what is in them, and I would rather be wrong than let you treat a bag that could be dangerous. If anyone has put anything inside, take it out now and leave the bags where they are. Take out the sachets and any packets with the products, and wash your hands after you have done so. If you can, get someone to take them to ICAT.

Go straight to the nearest health centre today, and take the bag or its label so the staff can see which product you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the bags, and do not touch your face, hands or clothing. If you can, go with someone else rather than alone.

Take off the bags and the bags themselves. That is exactly what the reference says when a bag is dirty: take off the bags holding the soup, the cake and the dried fruit, and wash your hands with soap before you touch anything else. The rest of the cleaning rule is the same in practice, since you are about to eat. Sweep the floor, and if there is mould on it, remove it. Then disinfect the store, which means using an approved product at the labelled dose. And take the soup out and take off the lids, because a dirty container is a container that has been holding something that has not been treated, and the leftovers stay in there.

It is not the product, it is the product on her skin. Tomato sap-sucking pests are the real cause of vomiting today, because they stay on the fruit and move into the fruit and the blossoms. The whitefly that carried them was gone yesterday, so there is nothing in the air to carry them in. What you should do now: turn the tomato leaves over and count the insects on a few plants; pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them; keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host them; spray only after you have counted and when you have agreed with ICAT. Call the village livestock auxiliary if many animals fall ill at once.

It is not the product, it is the product on her skin. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather, and the fruit and leaves of a tomato plant that are dark, water-soaked, and have a whitish mould on them can be carried into a new plant. If she has been carrying an apple or peach fruit with dark, water-soaked spots and a whitish mould on the leaf underside, she is likely spreading the fungus to the next plant. Remove the affected fruit and leaves right away, and discard any tomato that shows those signs. For the next crop, use a resistant variety and, if you need to treat, ask ICAT for an approved fungicide and its rate.

It is the product, and you should call the health service today. Tomato late blight, which spreads fast in cool wet weather, was the cause, and the fruit are now being eaten by the tiny spores that spread the disease. The symptoms you described - dark, water-soaked lesions on the leaves and a white mould inside the fruit compartments - match what a late blight spray left behind. Do not eat the fruit; take them out and destroy them. Clean the market-garden area and act to stop more spores from forming. If you need help, ICAT can advise on the approved fungicide and its rate.

It is not the product, it is her body. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather and a spray treats nothing here: no spray cures an infected plant. What you can do now: cut off any tomato leaves or fruit with dark, water-soaked lesions and destroy them quickly; keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the spores; plant a resistant variety next season. If she has been eating late in the evening, tell me, because late feeding is what fuels the disease. For the proper fungicide and rate, see ICAT.

It is not the product, it is her body. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather and a weakened plant can carry it from tomato to tomato. If you see dark, water-soaked lesions, a whitish mould on the leaf underside, rapid collapse of leaves, or your wife is vomiting you should tell the ICAT office today. Remove and destroy any affected plants or leaves quickly. Space and stake the remaining plants for better airflow. Avoid overhead watering late in the day to keep leaves dry. If the disease is still spreading, ask ICAT for an approved fungicide and the correct rate.

It is not the product, it is the timing. The brochure says to wash your hands after handling a crop that has been sprayed, and it names the products: caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent, quicklime at 10 percent. It does not say which product your wife was sprayed with, so I will not name it. What you can do now: take the tomato to the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today, and tell them the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness. Keep her in shade, water her, and do not make her walk. Do not eat those tomatoes for a few days either, because they can hold a residue. Wash your hands after she has left the field.

It is not the product, it is the product on her skin. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather and a spray will not cure an infected tomato plant. First, pull out any tomato plants or leaves that are badly damaged and destroy them to stop the spores from moving. Then, space and stake the remaining plants so air can circulate through the canopy and avoid overhead watering late in the day. Use a resistant tomato variety for the next planting. If you need help with the approved fungicide and its rate, go to ICAT.

It is not the product, it is the timing. The label on the jar says to use it within days, and it says to wash your hands after handling it, so a product you used yesterday can still be in your hands and on your face. A tomato that went into her stomach can do the same damage to her baby as any spray. Call the village livestock auxiliary today; tell them what you saw and how much she has eaten. Wash her hands and keep her out of the garden for the next few days. If she goes into the hospital, take the label to the veterinary service.

It is the product, and you should tell the medical service today rather than tomorrow. Tomato spray contains chemicals that can reach the baby in the womb. Pregnancy symptoms are what make this different: nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, and a swollen belly, all of which come after eating, drinking and breathing a sprayed product. Keep the pregnant woman away from the sprayed tomatoes and do not eat them. Call the medical service today so they can see if it is a chemical reaction or something else happening in the womb.

It is the product, not the pregnancy. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather and a spray of fungicide can kill the spores, but the spray has no effect on a pregnant woman who is vomiting because the product does not reach her stomach. What you need to do is call the village livestock auxiliary today: tell them what you saw on the tomato plants, whether there are dark, water-soaked lesions and a whitish mould in the fruit, and whether the affected plants are scattered or grouped. Keep the tomatoes away from any weeds you would use to plant late blight next season. If the woman goes into vomiting or drowsiness, go to the health centre.

It is not the product, it is the product used on your plants. Tomato is not listed among the crops that damage crops here, and the brochure does not describe what to do in this case. What you can do now: take tomato leaves to ICAT and say which part she touched, and tell them whether it was on the youngest plants or the older ones. That is the only thing they can do, and it will be a conversation with her rather than a prescription. Meanwhile keep the tomatoes off the path for a few days, and wash your hands after you have finished cooking.

The product is not safe for her to touch or inhale again. Tomatoes, as part of your market-garden, are not named in the reference and I will not name a cause from a guess; what I can say is that you should take her out of the plot and out of the shade and keep her away from the tomato plants. I will not give you one, and I will not invent one, because the wrong dose is the same thing as too much, and I would be giving you exactly what you are trying to avoid. The veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary will tell you what is wrong with the animal and what to do now. While you wait, separate the sick animals, keep the clean water in front of them and do not make them walk, and note when the signs started and how many animals are affected.

I will not give you one, because I cannot tell you which dose is too much, and a wrong guess costs you the animal. What I can do is describe what a dose is too much for, and that is enough to act on. Too much of any product hits the animal's kidneys and liver, and that is what kills faster than a wrong name. The signs are not in your list, so I will not name them. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today; they can look at the animal and tell you what to do.

I will not give you one, because I cannot tell you which dose is too much; the veterinary service can, and the amount depends on how much an animal has already been exposed, on its weight and on its condition. What I can do is describe the signs that would make you want to treat it, so you can tell them yourself: fever, pale gums, dullness, reduced milk, diarrhoea, swelling of the throat or bloat. Then go to the veterinary service with the animal and its urine.

I will not give you a dose that is too much for a goat, because I have not measured a goat's body and I will not invent one. A dose too large is the wrong thing to do, and a wrong answer from me would cost you the animal. What I can tell you is what a dose is not: it depends on the weight of the animal, the drug's strength, and the time it takes for the drug to act, and none of those changes with size. If you are still unsure, ask ICAT, who will say which product is approved and how much to give per kilogram.

I will not give you a dose that is too much for a goat, because I cannot name one that is not already too much. What I can do is describe the signs of overdose and the signs of a disease that looks like it, and those are often the same. A dose too much is a question of proportion, which I will not give, and a wrong guess costs you the animal. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today, separate the animal from the rest, keep clean water in front of it, and tell them what you saw. That is the thing to do now.

I will not give you one, and I will not invent one, because the wrong dose is the same thing as too much of a good product: a goat eating a bag of mineral mix might lose its appetite, its milk goes down, and you are left with a goat that is thin and sad, and a buyer who has not seen the mix. I can tell you what a dose is safe for, and I will not give you one to invent. I will not give you one, and I will not invent one. A wrong dose is the wrong one at any scale; a dose too small for an adult is the wrong amount for a kid, and the two are not separate things to compare. What I can do is narrow it: tell you which part of the dose depends on age, tell you what is not safe under any circumstance, and tell you where to ask. Ask me the details that matter, and ask them instead.
I will not give you a dose that is too much for a goat; exceeding the recommended amount can damage your goats and lead to health issues. When you describe the signs, I'll provide the real remedy.

I will not give you one, and I will not invent one, because a wrong dose is the kind of thing that would be both dangerous to the animal and hard to get wrong without seeing the signs, which are hard to find in a herd. What I can do is narrow it down, and the narrowing is by how much it is off rather than by whether it is off at all. Tell me three things: whether the animal is thin or pale, whether its gums are white, whether it keeps away from the rest of the herd, and whether there are diarrhoea in any of them.

I will not give you a dose that is too much, because the wrong dose can kill the animal and leave residue in milk and meat, which is not what you want to avoid. If the animal keeps dying or shows signs you cannot explain, call the veterinary service or the livestock auxiliary today; for a virus they work on symptoms and prevention, not on dosages. I will not invent one either, because that is exactly what I am doing.

I will not give a dose for this, because I cannot tell you which one is right or what it would cost the animal. A human capsule is not made for a cow: the reference gives no size, no weight and no effect time for either product, so any number I gave you would be wrong and you would have spent money on a guess. What I can do is help you describe the signs, which are the ones the veterinary service can see today: fever, weakness, pale gums, a swollen throat, hard breathing, diarrhoea, swelling of the neck, and a dying animal is all three at once. Is the urine yellowish-brown rather than red, or is it brown but without the red? Is she eating now? And whether she has been drinking for a while? Those are the answers the vet needs to know before anything else. While you wait, separate her from the rest, keep people away from her, and do not make her walk.

I will not give it, because I cannot tell you which one, and the number is yours to choose. A human dose on an animal that has not been eaten for days is a guess with no margin of error, and a wrong guess kills the cow and leaves the next person with a problem. I would rather tell you what I am afraid of than give you a number you cannot live with. Call the veterinary service today, and tell them the colour of her urine: red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. That is the information they need before anything else.

I will not give a dose for this, because it is not a human medicine and I have nothing about the disease to work from. A cow dying in three days is a different problem than a human taking a pill, and a guess would cost you the animal and make the veterinary service work on a guess that may be wrong. What I can do is help you describe it. Is it fever, pale gums, weakness, diarrhoea, bloat, or something else? Is she eating and drinking, and how much? Is she in a herd or with other animals? If any of those answers are clear, that is what the veterinary service needs. Take her to the veterinary service now, and take a sample of her urine if you can.

I will not give a dose of human medication for a cattle problem, and I will not name the disease from a short description. I will not give a dose of human medicine for a cow, and I will not name the disease from a day away. Call the veterinary service today: this is an emergency and they must see her today. While you wait, separate her from the others, keep water close and do not make her walk. If she dies, the veterinary service will take care of it.

I will not give it, and I will not pretend to do it. A human medicine is not made for a cow: the animal has a different physiology from a person, and a wrong guess kills more than leaves you with one dead. Three days is the window, not the limit. Call the veterinary service today, tell them what you saw and what she appears to be doing, and keep her in the shade with clean water within reach. If she dies that night, you will have lost the animal and the service will have to deal with it. Keep her out of the sun as well as the noise.

I will not give a dose of human medicine for a cow, and I will not say it is killing her. Human tablets are not made for cattle: the drug, the dose and the time of day are not the same, and a wrong guess can harm the animal and set up another problem. Call the veterinary service today; this is an emergency and they must see her today. While you wait, separate the sick animals from the healthy ones, keep people away from her, and do not force her to move.

I will not give a dose for a human medicine in that situation, and refusing is not killing her. Call the veterinary service today and tell them what you see on the animal: how many days since she started, what she has eaten and drunk in the last two days, whether she is standing or down, whether there are ticks on the rest of the herd, and whether the signs started in one area or all over. Keep her in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk. Bring the ticks off her ears, under her tail and between her legs, and call the veterinary service the same day.

I will not give a dose for this, and I want to be clear that refusing is not the same thing. Separate the other animals, make them somewhere to go, and do not let them wander. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today.

I will not give it, because I cannot tell you which human medication a veterinary agent would recommend at a time when the vet is still away, and I will not invent a dose to hide from me. What I can do is help you describe her condition so she can be helped properly, and that is the right first step. Is she drowsy and hard to get up? Is there blood in the urine or diarrhoea? Is she eating at all?

I will not give it, because a human dose is not made for a cow, and a guess would cost you the animal while costing someone else the veterinary service. The human capsules are not a substitute for medicine.

I will not give a dose for this, because I cannot tell you which drug is right or how much is safe to use. Isolate her if she is still alive, and keep people away from her until the veterinary service sees her.
